newsitem.title: KENYA: Aid groups said inflating Zaire crisis for funds.
newsitem.headline: Aid groups said inflating Zaire crisis for funds.

text.p: As the world lurched towards intervention in eastern Zaire, human rights activists on Wednesday accused some aid agencies of deliberately exaggerating the extent of the crisis to raise funds.
"The idea that a million people will die within weeks is absurd," said Alex de Waal of the London-based group Africa Rights which monitors human rights on the continent.
He said even at their height and over much longer periods, recent mass famines in Ethiopia and Somalia had claimed nothing like that number of lives.
"The idea that within days you will see rates of starvation three or four times higher than that is simply not being challenged," de Waal added.
De Waal and other aid experts say several aid groups were racing each other to get involved in the hope of attracting scarce funds from fatigued donors.

"They are focusing on refugees in the area to the exclusion of equally impoverished local people and people in other areas, such as Sudan...(but) for the fundraisers, this has simply been too good an opportunity to miss," he told Reuters.
Regional experts say several aid groups were also ignoring the role they played in helping create the conditions for the current crisis.

Hundreds of thousands of Hutu refugees flooded into eastern Zaire from Rwanda in 1994 following the victory of a Tutsi-led rebel movement which ended the genocide of an estimated 800,000 people, mainly Tutis and moderate Hutus.
Among those refugees, who have now fled fighting between Zairean Tutsi rebels and the army, were many involved in the slaughter carried out by then-Rwandan army and militia groups.
Several aid groups pulled out of the area after threats from Hutu thugs who took control of the camps, prevented people from returning to Rwanda, and plotted their own comeback.
"The critical issue of how to prevent a repetition of past errors is receiving scant attention," said one regional analyst, adding aid alone could not solve a political crisis.

That view echoes a recent report by 52 experts from 37 countries on the 1994 crisis. "Humanitarian action cannot substitute for political action," said the report coordinated by the development arm of the Danish Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

"A precondition for any solution to the crisis...is that the international community shows resolve and willingness to stop the killings, halt the supply of weapons to the region, and bring the killers to justice," it added.
Despite the 1994 experience and failed U.N. interventions in Bosnia and Somalia, regional experts said the international community was again set to become involved in a crisis in a policy vacuum.
Momentum behind a multinational force, which Canada has offered to lead, gathered pace on Wednesday, but clues as to what it would be empowered to do remained sketchy.

Emma Bonino, European Union Humanitarian Aid Commissioner, told the European Parliament there should be no delay: "If it arrives in three weeks time it will have a lot of work burying corpses but not much else."
She said aid corridors should be two-way and refugees should not be forced to return to Rwanda but should be disarmed to prevent an explosive situation in the camps.
In the past responsibility for disarming thugs fell on weak and often complicit local authorities and several likely contributors to the force are reluctant to take on that role.
"We are talking about peacekeeping not peace-enforcement," Kenya's Foreign Minister Kalonzo Musyaka told Reuters on Tuesday.
